newsitem.title: CHINA: H-shares - new darlings of Hong Kong stock market.
newsitem.headline: H-shares - new darlings of Hong Kong stock market.

text.p: Shares of mainland Chinese firms listed in Hong Kong, or H-shares, have surged more than 50 percent since China resumed sovereignty of Hong Kong on hopes of corporate restructuring.
Money from mainland China, local investors and foreign funds have been buying the sector, making H-shares the new darlings of the Hong Kong stock market, analysts said.
"It is a liquidity driven market -- liquidity flowing into the H-shares after the blue-chip rally," said Eugene Law, associate director at Lippo Securities.

The Hang Seng Chinese Enterprises Index jumped 94.75 points, or 6.61 percent, to close at 1,528.70 on Wednesday, outperforming the blue-chip Hang Seng Index, which gained 0.61 percent, and the red-chip index, which rose 2.93 percent.
The H-share index has soared more than 50 percent in the six weeks since Britain handed Hong Kong back to China on July 1, ending 156 years of colonial rule.

The rally has been principally driven by hopes of a wave of restructurings in China's state-owned companies that could boost the earnings of their Hong Kong-listed arms through asset injections or mergers, analysts said.
"Restructuring has given investors an excuse to speculate on H-shares," said Law.
Tackling the restructuring of the huge -- and flagging -- state sector is believed to be one of the major topics of China's 15th Party Congress to be held in September or October.

"The current enterprise reform they are talking about is a very large scale one which affects everybody, every Chinese enterprise," said Lawrence Ang, head of China research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
H-shares have been wallowing in a slump for about two-and-a-half years due to disappointing corporate earnings, but a gradual recovery began to take place at the beginning of the year.

However, it was not until Shanghai Hai Xing Shipping Co Ltd and Tsingtao Brewery Co Ltd announced in July that they were involved in corporate restructuring that H-shares became the focus of the market.

The concept of corporate restructuring is expected to replace the asset injection concept that has driven red chips -- shares of Hong Kong-based companies with Chinese parents -- as a main driving force of China-related companies, said Patrick Chia, research manager at China Everbright Securities.
"Asset injections among red chips has slowed down a bit recently. Enterprises reforms are expected to be a first priority among Chinese firms and that gives people a good buying excuse," he said.
Speculation that China's petrochemical industry will go through a major restructuring has boosted chemical counters such as Jilin Chemical Industrial Co and Yizheng Chemical Fibre Co Ltd.
Although analysts cast doubts on whether restructuring will be able to turn around the loss-making state-owned firms, they were optimistic for the longer term.

"If you look at the macro-economic side, the outcome of the 15th Party Congress -- all signs point to exciting measures," Ang said, adding that there were sufficient reasons for the sector to rise so much.
"It will not be surprising if profit-taking emerges in the short-term but on a six-month to one-year view, investors should see good returns even if they buy now," he added.
